how a pregnant woman's nutrition affects the health of her children.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of testosterone and androgens in general in the pathophysiology of prenatally induced hypertension is not well defined.
the role of androgens in prenatally programmed adult hypertension is not clear and requires further investigation.
the presence of testosterone in males does not prevent the development of prenatally induced hypertension in male rats but does appear to promote renal injury in these animals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
androgens are not necessary for programming hypertension in the LP males.
testosterone does not promote prenatally programmed high blood pressure, but it may contribute to the development of renal disease.
the male offspring of LP dams are more prone to develop hypertension and renal disease as adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the programming effect of undernutrition during pregnancy is not prevented by castration, and the sex differences in blood pressure and renal disease are not abolished by castration in adult life.

castration of male LP offspring failed to provide any protection against the hypertension that develops later in life, and this suggests that androgens are not the primary mediators of the sex difference in hypertension.
the sex difference in BP in this model of prenatally-programmed hypertension is not dependent on androgens.
